facts: I think my first experience with AI agents was around two years before the original interview, in response to the question on when I started using AI for programming.
But yeah.
For AI support specifically at work, I use only GitHub Copilot because that is the tool my company provides.
AI is always integrated into my IDE at work.
I mainly use AI support when I have a very big feature to implement.

For a large feature or technical problem, I ask AI for different possible approaches before deciding how to implement it. I ask what ways there are to solve the specific problem, compare the advantages and disadvantages AI gives, and choose myself. Much of our work instead concerns domain knowledge and business matters, where AI is not very useful.
At the original interview, I rarely used AI for writing or generating code at work.
I rarely use AI for code generation nowadays because our project has a mature code base and we mostly make small changes or improvements that can be done manually, rather than writing much new code.
I sometimes use AI for debugging.
Yeah.
I sometimes use AI to understand unfamiliar code or calls, as phrased in the source.
My team does not do much refactoring at the moment, but when I do refactor, I often use AI.
I often use AI when writing tests.
I sometimes use AI for documentation, but tend to prefer summarizing things myself.
I often use AI for explaining concepts or learning in general.
Yeah.G.Yes.

Before going on a short leave, I think my last task was building an MVP for a new API my team wanted to expose. It took roughly two weeks, possibly three or a little over two. I first talked to other teams to collect requirements and understand what they expected, before coding. I then worked on the API specification in my IDE, using AI to generate a basic specification blueprint I could modify. After that I added the endpoints agreed with the other teams.

For the new API MVP, I implemented each endpoint step by step. I decided which parts to build first; AI did not decide the order. When I faced specific implementation problems, such as whether a database call should use a transaction, I asked AI questions like a colleague sitting next to me and built the solution based on those answers.

While building the API MVP, I gradually sent code to my colleagues for review, usually endpoint by endpoint rather than the entire API. They reviewed the code and we built the API together; I also wrote tests while implementing it.

I do not remember using AI much to write the API tests. I mostly thought about the tests myself and, when facing a specific challenge, asked in chat how to solve that problem. I did not continually ask AI to generate tests for methods; I wrote the tests and decided the solution myself after asking for help when needed.
When I asked AI about a specific test-writing problem in the API MVP, I decided the solution myself.
Task definition in my team is a shared responsibility rather than being assigned to one person. During refinements, the team creates tickets together.
In team refinements, we create tickets specifying at a very high level what must be done, more like a list of things to remember.
We share tickets within the team, but they are not standalone instructions someone can simply pick up and implement. They are bullet-point to-do lists of things to remember.

A ticket alone is insufficient to solve a problem in my team; a developer must talk to people, understand the context and figure out a solution, because the ticket does not specify exactly what to do and how to do it.
Yeah.
Yeah.
I rated writing code in my general workday as sometimes.
I moved from the general writing-code activity to reviewing code; I rated reviewing code sometimes in my next answer.
I rated reviewing code as sometimes in my general working day.
I almost never spend time running tests manually in my general workday because our tests mostly run automatically.
I do specification work very often in my general working day.
I reaffirmed that specification is something I do very often.
I rated documentation as often in my general working day.
I rarely stop work to do an explicit learning activity such as a course; I revised my initial 'sometimes' answer on learning.
I agreed with the suggested change of my explicit learning frequency rating from sometimes to rarely.
Defining the specification for how to solve a problem takes up a large amount of my time, and is the activity I spend the most time on overall.
Compared with specification work, I usually spend relatively little time actually writing the code.
I spend much of my work time thinking about what needs to be built and how to build it, while the actual code to write is usually small in amount.

My team integrates our company's systems with third-party software by moving data between them. A typical request is to ingest a new data point, such as product prices, into the third-party platform. The difficult part is clarifying business requirements: which prices (per country, current-day or yearly average, for example), which data point, how frequently it is needed and which team exposes it. Once those specifications are agreed, implementation may take only five or ten lines of code. That
Yeah.

For integration work, one part involves talking to business people to obtain internal company knowledge. AI agents cannot solve those company-specific requirements questions. Once the requirements are established, I use AI to help find where the required data point is located.

To find a data point after defining the business requirements, I use a tool such as ChatGPT rather than IDE AI. For instance, SAP is widely used and documented online, so I can ask ChatGPT which SAP table provides product price data. I find this extremely helpful; before AI, I would have searched documentation myself or talked to someone with more SAP expertise.
Yes, I often need to work with code that I did not write.
I do not work much with unfamiliar parts of our code base, because I joined the team when no code had been written and have been there since the start, so I know what is happening in it.
I now normally need to read code written by other people, even though I have been in the team since the beginning.

My team has been implementing new capabilities involving machine-learning models to provide forecasts. This work started later while I was busy with other things, so I was not familiar with the machine-learning side. Someone asked me to review some of that code, and I did a high-level analysis of the pieces and how they worked together. I do not think I used AI because I did not need to understand all the details for that review.
When asked for another AI-assisted task, I recalled the examples already mentioned: using AI to learn about SAP and asking questions about problems I wanted to solve in the code base.
I considered documentation as another possible use of AI at work, but do not use AI for it very much.
Yeah.Yeah.
I could not think of any additional work task beyond the examples already mentioned, including any task that was AI-based from the beginning.
I could only think of the AI-use examples I had already described, with no further distinct example.
Yeah.Yes.
Before I started using AI, I performed similar tasks without AI at all.

My impression is that AI lets me explore a more complete set of potential solutions to a problem in less time. Without AI, researching and comparing all possible solutions would take longer; I might find one or two approaches and choose one without exploring others. I emphasize that this is my feeling rather than a measured result.

I decide whether to rely on AI-generated answers by judging them myself. I usually understand what AI is answering, and it is uncommon for me to see something entirely wrong; it often provides good and bad points about possible solutions, and I decide which approach I prefer.

I feel I need to check AI answers less and less. Around a year before the original interview, I recall more completely wrong or nonsensical answers; nowadays my impression is that there are fewer wrong answers, especially when asking questions in a smaller context.
My method of validating AI output is simply reading it; I do not use a special validation technique.
I write tests, but not specifically because of AI; I would write the same tests even if I had written the code myself.
I write tests so that someone who later changes the code can rerun them, not because I used AI.
I do not consider tests a specific method I use to validate AI's work.
Yeah.
Yeah.Yeah.

I do not think my team uses AI as much as the surrounding hype suggests. I use it as a helpful tool that makes us better and faster developers, but my workplace is not close to having AI generate code and do all the work. Much of our work relies on talking to people, other teams and business stakeholders and understanding company context. A ticket alone is insufficient; generating code is often the easiest and least time-consuming part. We use AI, but not excessively.
